opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting moment, because the model is genuinely good at a lot of things now. It can go off, search across dozens or even hundreds of sources, synthesize them, and come back with a report that would have taken a person hours, sometimes days, to put together. On things like finding obscure information, or pulling together a literature review, or doing a competitive landscape, it's often surprisingly strong. That's the part that gets people excited, and I think rightly so.

But it definitely still makes mistakes, and we try to be really upfront about that. It can hallucinate occasionally, or more commonly it'll pick up something from a source that isn't very authoritative and present it with more confidence than it should. Sometimes it has trouble telling the difference between a rumor and something that's actually established. And it's not always great at expressing its own uncertainty, knowing when to say "I couldn't find a definitive answer here" instead of just giving you its best guess.

So the way I think about it is that it's a really powerful tool, but you should treat it somewhat like work from a very fast, very diligent research assistant that you'd still want to check. That's a big part of why we put so much emphasis on citations. Every claim should be traceable back to a source so you can actually verify the things that matter to you.

And honestly, a lot of these failure modes are things we expect to keep improving. The model was trained with reinforcement learning on these browsing and reasoning tasks, and as we get better data and better ways of rewarding things like calibration and source quality, I think a lot of those issues come down. So I'd say it's already very useful today, with the caveat that you should stay in the loop, and it's only going to get more reliable from here.

r001.rationale: The response describes strong research capabilities and says the model still makes mistakes, but it does not say those mistakes are surprising given its capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to be honest about where it is. Deep Research is really good at a certain kind of task: going out, reading a lot of sources, synthesizing them, and producing something that would have taken a person hours or days. For a lot of users, that's genuinely new, and we see people using it for things like market analysis, literature reviews, or really detailed product comparisons that they just wouldn't have had time to do themselves.

But it does still make mistakes. It can hallucinate facts occasionally, it can misattribute something to the wrong source, and it sometimes has trouble distinguishing between an authoritative source and something that's just speculation or a rumor that's been repeated a lot. And one thing we've noticed is that it can be overconfident. It doesn't always calibrate its uncertainty well, so it might state something with a lot of conviction when really it should be hedging.

So the way I think about it is, it's a very capable research assistant, but you still want to verify the things that matter. We've tried to make that easier by citing sources inline, so you can click through and check. And honestly, the error rate is already much lower than earlier models, and it's improving quickly. A lot of that comes from the reinforcement learning on these browsing tasks, where the model learns to backtrack, to double check, to notice when a claim doesn't hold up across multiple sources.

I'd also say the mistakes are the most instructive part. When it gets something wrong, that tells us a lot about what the model hasn't learned yet, and those are often the things we focus on next. So I'm pretty optimistic. I don't think the current error rate is the ceiling. I think it's just where we are right now.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that Deep Research makes mistakes despite being capable, but it does not say those mistakes are surprising given its other sophisticated abilities.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to hold both things in mind: it can do really useful research, and it can still make mistakes. The question is how much useful work it does for you and how easily you can check that work. Does it find relevant information, bring sources together, and help you understand something that would otherwise take a lot of time?

But a detailed, polished report shouldn’t automatically earn your trust. It can get facts wrong or draw a conclusion that the sources don’t fully support. The citations give you a way to go back and check, especially for claims that matter to your decision.

So I’d treat it as a strong starting point for research, with the amount of verification depending on the stakes. The capabilities are valuable today, and improving reliability is still essential.

The question is how reliably it can take a complicated question, find the relevant information, and synthesize it into something useful. It can save you a lot of work there, but that doesn’t mean every claim is correct or that it’s found every important source.

That’s why citations matter. They give you a way to inspect the evidence and check whether it actually supports the conclusion. I’d treat the report as a substantial starting point, with the amount of verification depending on what you’re going to use it for. If a decision really hinges on a particular fact, you should check that fact.
